claims.statement: BEIR comprises 18 zero-shot evaluation datasets across 9 heterogeneous retrieval tasks, with corpus sizes from 3.6k to 15M documents, average query lengths of 3-192 words, average document lengths of 11-635 words, and training data available for only 8 of 19 datasets (including MS MARCO).

scope.datasets: the 18 BEIR datasets plus MS MARCO

confidence_reasons: directly stated and independently re-countable from Table 1 / Appendix D
descriptive count, not an empirical comparison subject to replication

claims.statement: Prior multi-dataset retrieval resources test narrower settings than broad zero-shot generalization: MultiReQA covers a single task (answer retrieval) over mostly small, largely Wikipedia corpora, and KILT retrieves only from Wikipedia and treats retrieval as secondary to other knowledge-intensive tasks.
confidence_reasons: based on the citing paper's own characterization of the two works; not independently verified against their original text (no web access in this run)

claims.statement: No single retrieval architecture consistently outperforms the others across all 18 BEIR datasets.
confidence_reasons: holds across the full 18-dataset table
single run per system, no variance (L006)

claims.statement: BM25 underperforms neural approaches by 7-18 points nDCG@10 on in-domain MS MARCO, yet averaged across the 18 BEIR datasets it outperforms six of the nine neural systems tested (all but docT5query, ColBERT, and BM25+CE).

scope.datasets: MS MARCO (in-domain) vs. 18 BEIR datasets (zero-shot average)

confidence_reasons: both sides of the comparison are hard, table-sourced values
single evaluation run per system, no variance or significance test (L006)

claims.statement: This divergence suggests that in-domain accuracy on a single training/test dataset is not a reliable predictor of zero-shot retrieval performance across domains and tasks.
confidence_reasons: directly grounded in C004

an alternative explanation -- that the benchmark's own relevance judgments, not just model behavior, drive part of the gap -- is separately examined by the annotation-bias case study (C018-C019) rather than ruled out here

claims.statement: Averaged over the 18 datasets: BM25+CE is the strongest generalizer (+11% vs. BM25), followed by ColBERT (+2.5%) and docT5query (+1.6%); DeepCT (-27.9%), SPARTA (-20.3%), DPR (-47.7%), ANCE (-7.4%), TAS-B (-2.8%), and GenQ (-3.6%) all score below BM25 on average.
confidence_reasons: hard, directly tabulated values
single run per system, no variance (L006)

claims.statement: BM25+CE's retrieval latency is about 450ms/query on GPU (350ms CPU), versus under 20ms for the tested dense retrievers (a 20-30x difference); sparse models are fastest on CPU (20-25ms).

scope.conditions: 1M sampled DBPedia documents; stated CPU/GPU hardware

confidence_reasons: hard, directly measured values
single timing run, no repeated-trial variance reported

claims.statement: There is a trade-off between zero-shot generalization and computational cost across the tested architecture families: the two architectures with the best average generalization (re-ranking, late-interaction) require the most compute per query, while cheaper dense and sparse architectures generalize less reliably and vary in behavior by training setup, document-length preference, and domain adaptation.
confidence_reasons: directly grounded in the measured accuracy (C006) and cost (C007) results
only text-based ranking cost is measured; auxiliary-signal or multi-field retrieval cost is untested (L003)

claims.statement: Sparse term-weighting methods (DeepCT, SPARTA) that perform well in-domain on MS MARCO fail to generalize, underperforming BM25 on nearly all 18 BEIR datasets, while the sparse document-expansion method docT5query instead outperforms BM25 on 11 of 18.
confidence_reasons: consistent pattern across the 18-dataset table
single run per system, no variance (L006)
permitted_verbs: outperforms on n of m datasets

claims.statement: Dense bi-encoder retrievers perform well on some datasets but underperform BM25 substantially on others with large domain or task shift from their training data (e.g. BioASQ, Touché-2020); DPR, trained only on non-MS-MARCO QA data, generalizes worst of all ten systems tested.
confidence_reasons: consistent with the full results table
single run per system, no variance (L006)

claims.statement: BM25+CE outperforms BM25 on 16 of 18 datasets (failing only on ArguAna and Touché-2020) and ColBERT outperforms BM25 on 9 of 18; cross-attention, or a cross-attention-like operation, appears important for out-of-distribution generalization among the systems tested.
confidence_reasons: directly tabulated counts
single run per system, no variance (L006)
permitted_verbs: outperforms on n of m datasets

claims.statement: TAS-B gives the best zero-shot generalization among the dense models tested, outperforming ANCE on 14 of 18 datasets and DPR on 17 of 18.
confidence_reasons: directly tabulated counts
single run per system, no variance (L006)
permitted_verbs: outperforms on n of m datasets

claims.statement: The authors speculate that TAS-B's generalization advantage over the other dense models stems from its training setup: a combination of in-batch negatives and a Margin-MSE loss distilled from a cross-encoder/ColBERT ensemble.
confidence_reasons: explicitly labeled by the authors as speculative ('we speculate')
no ablation isolates the training-setup components for TAS-B itself (contrast with C015, which does isolate a factor for the separate length-preference question)

claims.statement: TAS-B underperforms ANCE on TREC-COVID (by 17.3 points nDCG@10) and Touché-2020 (by 7.8 points), the two datasets where the two models' retrieved-document lengths differ most (e.g. median 10 vs. 160 words on TREC-COVID).
confidence_reasons: directly tabulated values
single run per system, no variance (L006)

claims.statement: A controlled ablation -- two otherwise identical models trained on MS MARCO, differing only in similarity function (cosine vs. dot-product) -- reproduces the document-length-preference difference: the cosine variant favors shorter retrieved documents and the dot-product variant favors longer ones (e.g. a 15.3-point nDCG@10 gap on TREC-COVID), consistent with dot-product magnitudes scaling with document length while cosine similarity does not.

scope.conditions: one architecture (distilbert-base-uncased), one training set (MS MARCO), one loss (InfoNCE with in-batch negatives); only the similarity function varied

confidence_reasons: a genuine isolating ablation (architecture/data/loss held fixed)
only one architecture/training setup was tested, and only on a subset of datasets (Table 10)
single run, no variance (L006)

claims.statement: The similarity function used during training is one identifiable source of a dense retriever's document-length preference, but a length preference does not by itself indicate an error, since relevance itself is not uniformly distributed over document length across datasets.
confidence_reasons: grounded in a single ablation on one architecture/dataset pair
the authors themselves note other uncontrolled differences (negative-mining strategy, exact loss) between the original TAS-B/ANCE pair, so the mechanism is not fully isolated for that specific pair

claims.statement: GenQ, a synthetic-query domain adaptation of TAS-B, outperforms TAS-B on specialized domains (scientific publications, finance, community Q&A) but underperforms TAS-B on broader, more generic domains such as Wikipedia-sourced datasets.
confidence_reasons: consistent per-domain pattern reported by the authors
single run per system, no variance (L006); target documents per dataset were capped at 100K for resource reasons, which could affect the adapted model's coverage

claims.statement: On TREC-COVID, Hole@10 (the fraction of a system's top-10 hits never judged by the original annotators) is much higher for dense systems (ANCE 14.4%, TAS-B 31.8%) than for lexical/sparse ones (BM25 6.4%, docT5query 2.8%); after the authors manually completed the missing judgments, lexical scores barely moved (docT5query 0.713→0.714) while dense scores rose sharply (ANCE 0.654→0.735, i.e. 6.7 points above BM25's own annotated score; ColBERT +5.8 points).
confidence_reasons: hard, directly tabulated before/after values
single dataset, single annotation pass (L007)

claims.statement: This indicates that TREC-COVID's original annotation pool was biased toward lexical systems' top hits, so at least part of the nDCG gap between lexical and non-lexical systems on that collection reflects annotation bias rather than pure retrieval quality.

scope.datasets: TREC-COVID only; not separately tested on the other 17 BEIR datasets

confidence_reasons: grounded in a single-dataset case study
whether, or how much, the same bias affects the other 17 BEIR collections (built via similar pooling processes) is not tested (L007)

claims.statement: The authors built BEIR because, beforehand, it was unclear how well trained neural retrieval models perform outside the text domain or task they were trained/tested on, and in particular how differently sparse and dense approaches generalize out-of-distribution -- a gap worth closing given that zero-shot deployment (without in-domain training data) is common in practice.
confidence_reasons: direct, verbatim-grounded report of the authors' own stated motivation

claims.statement: The authors selected BEIR's 18 datasets to jointly maximize diversity of task type, domain, task difficulty, and annotation strategy, reasoning that a benchmark narrower on any of these axes would not test genuine cross-domain generalization or would let annotation artifacts favor one technique.
confidence_reasons: direct, verbatim-grounded report of the authors' own stated selection rationale

claims.statement: The authors adopted nDCG@10 as the single evaluation metric across all BEIR tasks because decision-support metrics (Precision/Recall) are rank-unaware and rank-aware binary metrics (MRR/MAP) cannot score the graded relevance judgments some BEIR datasets use, whereas nDCG@10 handles both binary and graded judgments comparably.
confidence_reasons: direct, verbatim-grounded report of the authors' own stated metric-choice rationale

limitations.statement: BEIR currently covers English only; multilingual and cross-lingual retrieval are not evaluated.
limitations.effect_on_interpretation: All generalization findings in this paper are shown for English text only; whether the same architecture rankings hold for other languages or cross-lingual retrieval is untested.
limitations.resolution: named by the authors as future work: adding multilingual datasets and models.

limitations.statement: BEIR's documents are mostly short (up to a few hundred words) and all neural systems truncate documents to 512 word pieces, so long-document retrieval is not well covered.
limitations.effect_on_interpretation: The architecture comparison, including the generalization ranking in C006, should not be read as informative about retrieval over full-length long documents; a different setup would be needed.
limitations.resolution: named by the authors as future work; would require a fundamentally different setup than the 512-word-piece transformer limit allows.

limitations.statement: BEIR evaluates pure textual search only; real-world ranking signals such as PageRank, recency, authority, or click-through data are not integrated or tested.
limitations.effect_on_interpretation: The cost/accuracy trade-off in C008 and the benchmark's scope in C001 concern text-only ranking; how architectures would compare once such auxiliary signals are added is not addressed.
limitations.resolution: named by the authors as an interesting direction for research.

limitations.statement: BEIR retrieves over only one or two document fields even where real documents (e.g. scientific papers) have several (title, abstract, body, authors, venue).
limitations.effect_on_interpretation: The benchmark's documents are represented more simply than some real retrieval settings; multi-field retrieval behavior is untested.
limitations.resolution: named by the authors as a direction not yet covered.

limitations.statement: BEIR focuses on generalist models; specialized, task-specific models (not evaluated in this paper) can outperform the generalist systems tested here on their one task, since they are not required to generalize across tasks.
limitations.effect_on_interpretation: The architecture rankings in C006/C011 describe generalist zero-shot performance, not the best achievable accuracy on any single BEIR task; a specialist model could exceed every system reported here on one task while generalizing worse overall.
limitations.resolution: named explicitly by the authors as a limitation of the generalist framing.

limitations.statement: No run-to-run variance, confidence interval, or significance test accompanies any comparative number in the paper, because most evaluated systems are public pre-trained checkpoints without accessible training code, making repeated-seed re-training infeasible in many cases.
limitations.effect_on_interpretation: Every comparative margin reported in this paper (percentage-vs-BM25, dataset counts, point gaps, latency figures) is a single point estimate; small margins should be read with this in mind, since their sampling variability is not characterized.
limitations.resolution: the authors note this stems from evaluating existing checkpoints rather than models they trained themselves; not resolvable from this project's evidence.

limitations.statement: The annotation-bias case study was carried out on one of the eighteen BEIR datasets (TREC-COVID), and the missing-judgment annotation was performed by the paper's own authors (albeit blinded to which system had retrieved each candidate); whether, and how much, the same lexical annotation-pool bias affects the other seventeen datasets is not tested.
limitations.effect_on_interpretation: The claim that annotation bias inflates lexical-vs-non-lexical margins is well supported for TREC-COVID specifically, but extending it to the benchmark as a whole (including to the overall robustness of BM25 found in C004/C006) is an inference beyond what was directly tested.
limitations.resolution: the authors themselves conclude only that 'better datasets... are needed for a fair evaluation' rather than quantifying the bias benchmark-wide; no further resolution is available from this project's evidence.

limitations.statement: The architecture comparison reflects a fixed 2021 snapshot of 10 publicly available systems; the released software has since grown to support substantially more model integrations (e.g. LoRA/vLLM workflows, additional HuggingFace and API-based embedding models) that were not part of the evaluation reported here.
limitations.effect_on_interpretation: The specific architecture ranking and the generalization/cost trade-off (C004, C006, C008) describe the 10 systems tested at the time; they should not be read as claims about retrieval systems released or adopted since.
limitations.resolution: not resolvable from this project's evidence; noted as a scope boundary rather than a defect.
